title: The Reading Skill We Desperately Need
author: Colton Cauthen
summary: Colton Cauthen opens with the provocative claim that almost no one on the internet is actually disagreeing, and then defines disagreement narrowly as knowingly holding a position contrary to another's about a matter of fact. Because disagreement requires accurate prior understanding, most online contention is really a quarrel with one's own misreading. He argues that learning to disagree well is essential to the pursuit of truth and even to the survival of Western civilization, and that its absence yields polarization, ignorance, and a kind of ugliness Socrates noted in opinion without knowledge. His remedy draws on Mortimer Adler's How to Read a Book: good books are the best training ground because they are carefully crafted, allow unlimited time for analysis, and remove the social pressure to perform. The piece closes with Adler's three maxims for critical reading and four legitimate grounds of criticism.
points: Cauthen defines genuine disagreement as knowingly holding a contrary position on a matter of fact, excluding mere differences of taste.
He argues that disagreement without understanding is really disagreement with one's own misconstruction of the other person's view.
Books are presented as the ideal training ground because they are edited, allow unhurried analysis, and are private enough to make admitting error easier.
Following Adler, a legitimate criticism must show an author is uninformed, misinformed, illogical, or incomplete.
quotes: To disagree with someone is to knowingly hold a position contrary to that of the other person about a matter of fact.
You cannot have a bona fide disagreement with someone until you understand their position. Otherwise, your disagreement is not with them, but with yourself
Learning how to disagree is an essential skill for anyone pursuing knowledge, wisdom, and understanding. It may also be vital to the survival of Western civilization in the long run.
In Plato's Republic, Socrates remarks that there is an ugliness to opinions without knowledge. There is also an ugliness to contention without understanding.
Reading comments left on YouTube videos and Substack articles, I often see people saying in effect, "I don't know what you mean, but I couldn't disagree more.
It is generally difficult to admit that we are wrong. It is probably at least a little easier to admit it to yourself than to or in front of other people.
If you cannot show how an author has failed in one or more of these ways, then your criticism regarding the truthfulness of the work is groundless.
